newsitem.title: UK: UK's OFFER says price restraints feasible.
newsitem.headline: UK's OFFER says price restraints feasible.

text.p: Britain's electricity industry regulator OFFER said on Thursday it believed maximum price restraints were feasible and better than cost pass-through controls in a competitive electricity market.

OFFER, in its fourth consultation paper on price arrangements for the market from April 1998 onwards, said the proposed restraints would last for two years and cover all domestic customers and businesses with annual demand under 12,000 kWh.
A statement from OFFER said calculations suggested average costs of 7.2 pence per kiloWatt hour (kWh) for a standard domestic customer, implying an annual bill of about 238 stg excluding tax.
"This represents a significant reduction on present tariffs," OFFER said.
OFFER said it had used a range of real reductions between four and 12 percent in prices for the electricity wholesale market or pool over the next three years.

OFFER said that supply business costs could be cut by a further 1.5 percent per year while a further margin of about 1.5 percent on turnover "might be appropriate to cover working capital and volume risk."
OFFER said delays in opening up markets to competition could be compensated through a percentage rebate to customers from price restrained revenue.

OFFER said it would consider limiting joint ventures between regional electricity companies (Recs) and major generators "to avoid the adverse effects of vertical integration," in an effort to aid competition.
The watchdog said it would also consider requiring Recs to pre-notify and justify price changes and to publish indicative use of system charges.
Comments on the consultation paper should be submitted by July 21, OFFER said.
